section_title: What does Mephibosheth say about Ziba’s accusation?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 24 Then Mephibosheth, Saul’s grandson, went down to meet the king. He had not cared for his feet or trimmed his mustache or washed his clothes from the day the king had left until the day he returned safely. 25 And he came from Jerusalem to meet the king, who asked him, “Mephibosheth, why did you not go with me?” 26 “My lord the king,” he replied, “because I am lame, I said, ‘I will have my donkey saddled so that I may ride on it and go with the king.’ But my servant Ziba deceived me, 27 and he has slandered your servant to my lord the king. Yet my lord the king is like the angel of God, so do what is good in your eyes. 28 For all the house of my grandfather deserves death from my lord the king, yet you have set your servant among those who eat at your table. What further right, then, do I have to keep appealing to the king?”

29 The king replied, “Why say any more? I hereby declare that you and Ziba are to divide the land.” 30 And Mephibosheth said to the king, “Instead, since my lord the king has safely come to his own house, let Ziba take it all!”

context_lines: Mephibosheth comes to meet David, having neglected his feet, mustache and clothing throughout the king’s absence. David asks why he did not accompany him. Mephibosheth says that Ziba deceived him when he wanted a donkey prepared and then slandered him.

He recalls David’s kindness in giving him a place at the royal table and submits the matter to the king. David ends the discussion by ordering that he and Ziba divide the land. Mephibosheth answers that Ziba may have it all, since David has returned safely.
common_interpretation_lines: [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-second-book-of-samuel/) reads Mephibosheth’s neglected appearance as mourning that supports his account of loyalty. The scene gives him the opportunity to answer the accusation David accepted in [2 Samuel 16:1–4](https://biblehub.com/bsb/2_samuel/16.htm).

[Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-second-book-of-samuel/) and [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/19.htm) understand the division as returning to the earlier arrangement in which Ziba works the estate and shares its proceeds. The BSB states David’s ruling directly without explaining all its practical terms. The narrative also gives no further hearing in which Ziba answers the charge of slander.

[Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/2_samuel/19.htm) emphasizes Mephibosheth’s joy at the king’s return. Whatever happens to the land, his final words place David’s safety above winning the dispute. That is the loyalty his reply expresses.
